extracted.intended_audience: public relations counsels; PR practitioners; communications professionals; journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and standards for public relations counsel on forming and influencing public opinion, focusing on group psychology, media selection, timing, and tactics. Useful for planning campaigns, messaging strategy, and institutional communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlist the established point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: “The moulder of public opinion must enlist the established point of view.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work with, enlist, or appeal to the public’s existing viewpoints and traditions rather than trying to impose a wholly foreign perspective. The text notes that editors/newspapers must consider the public which buys the paper (Mencken) and gives examples where newspapers have deliberately maintained a point of view that is hostile or cold among parts of the public. Occasional bravery (e.g., the Baltimore Suns) can alter public opinion, but enlistment of existing points of view is the normal practical route.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study the mirrors of the public mind (media & platforms)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Study of the mirrors of the public mind--the press, the motion pictures, the lecture platform and the others--reveal to him what their standards are and those of the groups they reach.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze the standards, conventions, and audiences of each medium you will use. Different media serve different constituencies and have their own selection conventions; understanding these lets you place messages where they will be accepted and effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discover stimuli to which public opinion responds
rubrics_metrics.description: “He must discover what the stimuli are to which public opinion responds most readily.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the emotional, cultural, social, or practical triggers that elicit response from target groups. Examples: Safety First used posters, lectures, films, safety weeks; effective campaigns capitalize on the specific stimuli a public already responds to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquire thorough knowledge of individual and group psychology
rubrics_metrics.description: “A fundamental study of group and individual psychology is required before the public relations counsel can determine how readily individuals or groups will accept modifications of viewpoints or policies.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground strategy in psychological principles (stereotypes, herd/crowd behavior, instincts). Use these to predict receptivity, resistance, and likely routes of persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and work with stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Stereotypes are shorthand images that 'largely determine what group of facts we shall see and in what light we shall see them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map prevailing stereotypes in the audience (e.g., roles like 'capitalist', 'woman lawyer') and use or counter them consciously. Stereotypes shape perception and selection of facts; campaigns must account for these entrenched patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and leverage crowd/herd dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowd/herd states of mind are pervasive; the herd exhibits homogeneity, intolerance of solitude, sensitivity to the herd voice, susceptibility to leadership, and dependence on recognition as a herd member.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design messaging that leverages herd tendencies: provide leadership cues, create a sense of group membership, use contests/boosting to capture attention, and present suggestions as aligned with herd norms. Recognize that herd suggestibility makes some propositions acceptable only when they appear to come from the herd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use diverse appeals and multiple channels
rubrics_metrics.description: The Safety First movement used 'every form of appeal, from poster to circular, from lecture to law enforcement, from motion pictures to “safety weeks.”'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ a coordinated mix of channels and formats (print, film, posters, lectures, events, enforcement) to reinforce messages and reach different segments of the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine research/analysis with public education
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rockefeller Foundation changed habits 'by analysis, investigation, applied medical principles, and public education.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support persuasive campaigns with credible research, investigation, and applied expertise. Pair facts and analysis with clear educational outreach so audiences can accept and adopt new behaviors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limitations and the importance of timing; you cannot manufacture public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: “The public relations counsel is not needed to persuade people to standardize their points of view ... he cannot manufacture it from thin air.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess realistically what can be influenced given prevailing attitudes and timing. Examples: Margaret Sanger succeeds with receptive audiences; Madam Curie’s impact depended on prior public preparation. Avoid expecting immediate conversion where group predispositions are strongly opposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align message with group traditions and shared reactions before seeking change
rubrics_metrics.description: “The cause he represents must have some group reaction and tradition in common with the public he is trying to reach. This must exist before they can react sympathetically upon one another.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure there are pre-existing affinities, traditions, or common reactions between the issue and the target public. If such common ground is lacking, build it slowly or seek receptive subgroups first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the bidirectional interaction between institutions and the public
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions 'make public opinion conform to the demands of the public' and the public 'responds to an equally large degree to these institutions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan strategies that account for both how institutions shape public opinion and how public sentiment constrains institutions. Successful campaigns work within this interaction rather than assuming unilateral influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor selection, emphasis, and framing to the audience’s standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection of news and prominence affects thought: 'Every newspaper when it reaches the reader is the result of a whole series of selections ... There are no objective standards here. There are conventions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control framing (what to highlight, placement, space, emphasis) to fit the expectations and attention patterns of your target constituency. Use appropriate prominence and angle to influence perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage leaders and opinion-makers tactically
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders 'live with their ears to the ground for every slight rumbling of public sentiment' and are important intermediaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify, brief, and work with leaders/opinion-makers who can amplify messages. Recognize leaders are responsive to public sentiment and can intensify or dissipate sympathy; they are rarely creators of sentiment from nothing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overcome the 'censorship' of the group mind
rubrics_metrics.description: “Propaganda is a purposeful, directed effort to overcome censorship--the censorship of the group mind and the herd reaction.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design directed persuasive efforts that bypass or counteract internal barriers (prejudice, entrenched beliefs) through credible messengers, framing, gradual exposure, or appealing to subgroup norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use news cycles and timing strategically: when real news breaks, semi-news yields
rubrics_metrics.description: From the Tribune advertisement: 'When real news breaks, semi-news must go. When real news is scarce, semi-news returns to the front page.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schedule releases and events to avoid being crowded out by major news; exploit slow news periods for greater prominence. Understand that competing events determine what will be noticed on a given day.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be consistent and, when appropriate, courageous in message and policy stance
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples where newspapers (e.g., the two Baltimore Suns, the World campaigns) 'have courageously and consistently stood for the policies of their editors and have refused to yield to pressure.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency and firmness can persuade over time and win respect; occasional public bravery (refusing to yield to pressure) can shift opinion, but expect resistance and weigh risks.
